title.narrative: Output 3.2. Increased capacity of member States to formulate and implement policies and strategies for creating decent work in the rural economy

description.narrative:
Through tripartite and inter-ministerial dialogue engaging the Ministry of Labour (MoL), the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) and the social partners, the Government of Jordan (GoJ) adopted the Agricultural Workers Bylaw No. 19 of 2021, that clarifies the labour rights and entitlements of agriculture workers and aims to improve working conditions in the agriculture sector. Among other improvements, the bylaw includes provisions for maternity leave for women agricultural workers. In addition, the Ministry of Labour has put in place measures to operationalize this legislative measure with a view to improve working conditions of rural women in floriculture.
In coordination with the MoL (Inspection Department) and MoA, a self-inspection checklist for farmers was made operational to improve labour inspection in agriculture, with particular attention to gender issues. The checklist was used as a reference point to respond to an article of the agriculture workers bylaw, which indicates that the MoL will develop inspection mechanisms for the agriculture sector. The checklist has also been shared with other UN and multilateral agencies (World Bank) and International NGOs (Agence d'Aide a la Cooperation Technique et au Developpement [ACTED], Mercy Corps, Centre for the Promotion of Imports from Developing Countries [CBI]) as a reference to monitor working conditions.
The recommendations of the joint ILO-Fafo-UNDP study on the Impact of COVID-19 on enterprises in Jordan informed the operationalization of the agricultural bylaw and the checklist bearing in mind the impact of the pandemic on agricultural and rural enterprises, as well as subsequent policy and programming formulation aiming at a human-centred recovery from the COVID-19 crisis. The ILO supported policy dialogue, empirical evidence and guidance in the drafting of the Agricultural Workers Bylaw No. 19 of 2021. The ILO carried out preliminary assessments on decent work deficits in agriculture to identify gaps in legislative coverage for agriculture workers, with recommendations to address them. Then, through the tripartite-plus technical committee on Agriculture established in 2019 with ILO's technical support, the ILO facilitated dialogue with agriculture workers and employers (farmers), consultations with cooperatives, and inter-ministerial dialogue between the Ministry of Labour and Ministry of Agriculture to provide inputs to and review proposed legislation for the sector. Based on the assessments, the ILO drafted an inspection checklist, using the Better Work checklist as reference.
With support from the Australian government, the ILO trained 36 labour inspectors (including women labour inspectors) on applying the new Agricultural Workers Bylaw to the agricultural sector, focusing on the floriculture subsector, in Irbid, Madaba, and Mafraq. The ILO trained 18 farmers (including women farmers), who represent employers, on the new bylaw in order to improve their understanding and implementation of decent work, which would in turn improve their export opportunities. The ILO organized a dialogue between labour inspectors and farmers to encourage cooperation in applying the new bylaw.
